title: 2 Kings 8:7–15
context: Elisha comes to Damascus while Ben-hadad king of Syria is sick. The king sends Hazael with a lavish gift to ask whether he will recover. Elisha’s answer is unusual: Hazael is to tell the king, “You will surely recover,” yet the LORD has shown Elisha that the king will surely die (8:10). The text does not explain this tension; readers commonly take it to mean that the illness itself would not kill the king, even though he would not live, and this page leaves the wording as it stands without proposing an alternative text. Elisha fixes his gaze on Hazael and weeps, foreseeing the harm Hazael will do to Israel (8:11–12), including atrocities against civilians that are reported here soberly and without elaboration. Hazael’s accession fulfills the commission given earlier to Elijah to anoint Hazael king over Syria (1 Kings 19:15), and the later narrative records Hazael’s attacks on Israel (2 Kings 10:32; 13:3, 22). On the next day the king is smothered with a wet cloth, and Hazael takes the throne (8:15). On how God’s foreknowledge relates to human responsibility, both traditions affirm that God knew Hazael’s deeds beforehand and that Hazael remained fully accountable; the difference in how foreknowledge relates to God’s decree is already treated elsewhere on the site (for example at Deuteronomy 31:21 and Exodus 3:19), so no new contrast box is added here.

verses.text: Elisha came to Damascus; and Benhadad the king of Syria was sick. He was told, “The man of God has come here.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha comes to Damascus while Ben-hadad, the king of Syria, is sick. Arminian readers note the reach of Elisha’s reputation, even among Israel’s enemies. The narrative moves into foreign affairs, showing that the LORD’s word through his prophet concerns the nations as well as Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s sovereignty extending beyond Israel’s borders, as he directs his prophet to Damascus. This recalls the commission concerning Hazael given to Elijah (1 Kings 19:15). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the LORD rules over the nations and their kings.

verses.text: The king said to Hazael, “Take a present in your hand, and go meet the man of God, and inquire of the LORD by him, saying, ‘Will I recover from this sickness?’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Ben-hadad sends Hazael with a gift to ask the man of God whether he will recover. Arminian readers note that even a foreign king who besieged Samaria seeks the LORD’s word through Elisha when facing illness. The request reflects respect for the prophet’s authority.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony of Israel’s enemy inquiring of the LORD through Israel’s prophet. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as recognizing that the LORD’s word carried weight even among the nations, and both note that the king’s question about his recovery sets up Elisha’s difficult answer.

verses.text: So Hazael went to meet him and took a present with him, even of every good thing of Damascus, forty camels’ burden, and came and stood before him and said, “Your son Benhadad king of Syria has sent me to you, saying, ‘Will I recover from this sickness?’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Hazael brings an extravagant present, forty camels’ burden, and calls Ben-hadad Elisha’s “son.” Arminian readers note the respect and urgency conveyed by the gift and the language. The narrator lets the reader see Hazael before learning what he will become.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the size of the gift and the deferential address. Hazael appears as a loyal servant at this point in the story. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as setting the scene for Elisha’s revelation, with no doctrinal point resting on the gift itself.

verses.text: Elisha said to him, “Go, tell him, ‘You will surely recover;’ however the LORD has shown me that he will surely die.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha tells Hazael to report, “You will surely recover,” but adds that the LORD has shown him the king will surely die. Arminian readers note that the text does not explain the tension; many take it to mean the illness would not be fatal, though Ben-hadad would still die. Hazael is told the truth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the difficulty and commonly read it the same way: the sickness would not kill the king, but he would not live. God knows the outcome fully. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with care, avoid accusing the prophet of deception, and leave unexplained what the text leaves unexplained.

verses.text: He settled his gaze steadfastly on him, until he was ashamed. Then the man of God wept.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha fixes his gaze on Hazael until Hazael is ashamed, and then the man of God weeps. Arminian readers see genuine grief at the harm Hazael will freely choose to inflict on Israel. The prophet’s tears show that foreknowledge of evil does not make it any less sorrowful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see real anguish in Elisha’s tears, and they note that knowing God’s purpose does not remove compassion for those who will suffer. Shared ground: both traditions see the prophet’s grief as fitting, and both affirm that God’s foreknowledge does not make the coming evil any less evil.

verses.text: Hazael said, “Why do you weep, my lord?” He answered, “Because I know the evil that you will do to the children of Israel. You will set their strongholds on fire, and you will kill their young men with the sword, and will dash their little ones in pieces, and rip up their pregnant women.”
verses.arminianNotes: Hazael asks why Elisha weeps, and Elisha names the violence Hazael will bring on Israel, including atrocities against children and pregnant women. Arminian readers report this soberly: the deeds will be Hazael’s own, and he remains fully responsible for them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the prophecy soberly, noting that 2 Kings 13:3 later says the LORD delivered Israel into Hazael’s hand, without excusing Hazael’s cruelty. Shared ground: both traditions refuse to soften or sensationalize the words, affirm Hazael’s guilt, and see the prophet’s grief as the right response to such evil.

verses.text: Hazael said, “But what is your servant, who is but a dog, that he could do this great thing?” Elisha answered, “The LORD has shown me that you will be king over Syria.”
verses.arminianNotes: Hazael protests that he is only a “dog,” and Elisha replies that the LORD has shown him Hazael will be king over Syria. Arminian readers see foreknowledge that does not compel Hazael’s choices; his ambition and cruelty will be his own, as the next verses show.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s knowledge as rooted in his sovereign purpose over the nations (1 Kings 19:15), while Hazael remains accountable. Shared ground: both affirm God’s exact knowledge of the future and Hazael’s responsibility; how foreknowledge relates to decree is treated in the existing box at Deuteronomy 31:21.

verses.text: Then he departed from Elisha, and came to his master, who said to him, “What did Elisha say to you?” He answered, “He told me that you would surely recover.”
verses.arminianNotes: Hazael returns and tells Ben-hadad only that he would surely recover. Arminian readers note that he passes on part of Elisha’s message while withholding the rest, a choice that reveals his intentions. The narrator lets his selective report speak for itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly note Hazael’s partial report and see the narrator preparing for his act in the next verse. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as revealing Hazael’s character through what he says and leaves unsaid, with responsibility for his deception resting on him.

verses.text: On the next day, he took a thick cloth, dipped it in water, and spread it on the king’s face, so that he died. Then Hazael reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: The next day the king is smothered with a wet cloth, and Hazael reigns in his place. Arminian readers read this plainly as murder, chosen by Hazael. The prophet’s foreknowledge did not cause the deed; Hazael seized the throne by violence and bears the guilt for it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Hazael’s act as a real crime for which he is accountable, even as it falls within the purpose announced earlier (1 Kings 19:15). Shared ground: both traditions report the killing soberly without expanding it, affirm Hazael’s guilt, and see the LORD’s word about Syria’s throne fulfilled.
